articles.title: Plans for New Car Wash at Former Paul Price Cars Site Refused by Rochdale Council
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has refused plans for a new car wash and laundrette at the former Paul Price Cars site on Kingsway, despite initial recommendations for approval.
articles.content_html:
A proposal to establish a car wash and laundrette at the former Paul Price Cars site, located at 311 Kingsway, Rochdale, has been refused by the planning committee of Rochdale Council. The application, submitted by Matthew Gray, sought to demolish the existing building and create five jet-wash bays, alongside facilities for a laundrette, dog wash, and vending machine.

Initially, planning officers recommended the application for approval, citing that it would positively utilise a site currently considered a blight on the surrounding area. Supporting documents argued that the development would align with relevant policies and improve the visual impact of the location compared to its current state.

However, the planning committee ultimately decided against the proposal, which has raised questions about the future of the site. The refusal means that the area will remain unchanged for the time being, continuing to detract from the visual appeal of Kingsway.

The next steps for the applicant remain unclear, as they may consider revising the proposal or appealing the decision. Local residents and businesses will be keen to see how this development unfolds, particularly given the site's potential for revitalisation.

articles.title: Roadworks on Greenhill Road in Middleton to Begin on 2 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks on Greenhill Road in Middleton will commence on 2 November 2026, affecting traffic and parking in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has confirmed that roadworks will take place on Greenhill Road in Middleton from 7.30am on Monday, 2 November 2026, until 6pm on Friday, 6 November 2026.

During this period, no waiting will be permitted at any time along the northern side of Greenhill Road. The restriction will start at the junction with Vicarage Lane and Church Road, extending 54 metres down the road in a south-easterly direction, ending outside 49a Greenhill Road.

Local residents and motorists should be aware of these restrictions, as they may impact parking and traffic flow. It is advisable to plan alternative routes if necessary during the roadworks period.

For further details and to view a map of the roadworks, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Lifts Out of Service at Freehold Tram Stop Until Further Notice
articles.excerpt: The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are currently out of service due to replacement works, affecting journeys towards Manchester and Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are out of service as of 6:59pm on Sunday, 18 October 2026, due to ongoing lift replacement works. This affects both platforms, with the lift towards Manchester and the lift towards Rochdale currently unavailable.

Passengers are advised to alight at either South Chadderton or Westwood tram stops and use the orange call point located at all stops to request assistance for completing their journeys. For further assistance, customers can contact the helpline at 0161 244 1000, which operates from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

The duration of the lift outage is currently unspecified, and no further updates have been provided regarding when the service will resume. Passengers are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel.

Transport for Greater Manchester apologises for any inconvenience caused by this disruption and is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Power Outage in Newhey Linked to 'Third-Party Interference'
articles.excerpt: Residents in Newhey experienced a power outage following a loud bang, attributed to third-party interference on the electricity network, with some left without power for three hours.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Newhey, Rochdale, were left without power for approximately three hours following a loud bang linked to an incident on the electricity network. The disruption occurred on the evening of October 18, as reported by Electricity North West.

The company stated that the power loss was due to 'third-party interference' on their high-voltage network. A message from Electricity North West indicated that investigations revealed the fault coincided with the loud bang heard at a property on Ogden Lane.

While most residents had their power restored by 23:17, one customer remained without supply as further investigations were necessary to ensure safety before restoration could occur. Electricity North West expressed appreciation for the patience of those affected during the investigation process.

The incident highlights the potential vulnerabilities in local infrastructure and the impact of external factors on essential services. Residents are encouraged to check official channels for updates regarding the restoration of power.

articles.title: The priest, the cock and the shoe: the Clegg Hall boggart that won’t lie down
articles.excerpt: The old tale of the Clegg Hall boggart is a durable piece of Lancashire storytelling; the building and its ownership are historical, the murder story is not.
articles.summary: The old tale of the Clegg Hall boggart is a durable piece of Lancashire storytelling; the building and its ownership are historical, the murder story is not.
articles.body:
On a winter night long ago, so the telling runs, villagers begged a pious man to speak with the restless spirits of Clegg Hall. The boggarts agreed to quit the place in return for “a body and a soul.” The monk answered with a riddle: bring him the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe. The two items were burned, the bargain sealed — at least for a while. The detail about the cock’s body and the shoe’s sole is printed in nineteenth‑century collections of Lancashire lore and is the punchline most locals still pass on. ([en.wikisource.org](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Lancashire_Legends%2C_Traditions%2C_Pageants%2C_Sports%2C_%26c./Part_1/The_Clegg_Hall_Tragedy))

Clegg Hall itself stands on Clegg Hall Road, between Smithy Bridge and Littleborough; the present house dates to about 1610 and is a Grade II* listed building. The official Historic England listing describes the stone house, its porch and mullioned windows and notes the hall’s architectural and documentary record rather than the supernatural tales attached to it. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

The story is folklore, collected and retold by Victorian antiquarians and local writers rather than drawn from contemporary legal or parish records. John Roby included a version in his Traditions of Lancashire and the Clegg Ho’ boggart also appears in Lancashire folk‑lore compilations; one local ballad, attributed to William Nuttall, dramatises the crimes and names a murderous uncle called Sir Roland. But the nineteenth‑century commentators themselves warn that Roby and others stitched patchy oral fragments into a romantic narrative, not an objective chronicle. In short: the tale survives as lively oral tradition and literary reworking, not as a contemporaneous record of a proven crime. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

That pattern — a local ghost-story collected in the nineteenth century, expanded by poets and antiquarians, then re-entered into the popular imagination — is typical of many English “boggart” traditions. Collectors such as Harland and Wilkinson treated the Clegg Hall boggart as a regional example of a household spirit story, noting variants and the way tellings changed over time. The cock‑and‑shoe trick, where a substitute is offered to satisfy a demand for a human sacrifice, is exactly the kind of folkloric device that marks a story as ritual or symbolic rather than documentary. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/41148/41148-h/41148-h.htm))

What we can verify: the house, its date and status on the National Heritage List; the survival of the legend in printed collections; and the role of Roby and local balladeers in popularising the version with the priest’s substitution. What we cannot verify from contemporary evidence is the core historical crime often told behind the haunting — no extant court record or parish entry from the medieval or early‑modern period proves the murder of heirs as related in later accounts. The reliable documentary record for the site is architectural and genealogical; the grotesque episodes belong to oral and literary tradition. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

For readers who like to see places: Clegg Hall is a protected historic house on private land; the Historic England entry is the place to start for architectural facts. If you want to read the original tellings, Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the nineteenth‑century Lancashire folk‑lore compilations are available online from digitised collections and show how the story was recorded and reshaped. If you prefer the supernatural to be unsettled, you can still repeat the line about the cock and the shoe and watch people’s faces; if you want a documented crime to go with it, the archives won’t oblige. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))
